chapters.title: Chapter 4: How Liquidity Moves Asset Classes

lessons.title: Crypto and the Liquidity Beta Trade: Bitcoin as a High-Beta Risk Asset

body.text: The "digital gold" narrative says Bitcoin should behave like an uncorrelated store of value. The data says something different: Bitcoin has traded far more like a high-beta version of the Nasdaq, amplifying global liquidity swings in both directions, not hedging against them.

children.text: A professional does not evaluate an asset by its marketing narrative. Bitcoin is often described as digital gold, implying it should hold value or even rise when other risk assets fall. Its actual price behavior since 2020 has mostly told a different story: a high correlation with growth-tech equities and a tendency to fall harder than the broader market during liquidity tightening, not less.

body.caption: 2022: A Global Tightening Year, Three Very Different Outcomes

cells: Amplified the risk-off move well beyond equities, consistent with high beta to liquidity
A genuine growth-equity liquidity drawdown, as covered in the previous lesson
Held up far better, consistent with central bank buying offsetting rising real rates, as covered in the previous lesson

body.text: Return figures are approximate, calendar-year, and drawn from widely reported market data. Exact figures vary slightly by data source and by the specific dates used.

body.caption: Beta measures how much an asset amplifies (beta greater than 1) or dampens (beta less than 1) moves in a reference market. Bitcoin's beta to risk assets like the Nasdaq has historically run well above 1, especially during liquidity-driven moves.

children.text: Why Crypto Amplifies Rather Than Hedges

Three structural features explain the high beta. First, crypto's investor base overlaps heavily with the same speculative, risk-on capital that buys high-growth tech stocks, so the two tend to be bought and sold by similar hands at similar moments. Second, crypto markets carry unusually high leverage through perpetual futures and on-chain borrowing, which mechanically amplifies moves in both directions through forced liquidations. Third, unlike gold, crypto has no multi-generational central bank or institutional holding base acting as a demand floor during stress, so there is little structural buying to cushion a liquidity-driven drawdown the way central bank gold purchases did in 2022.

body.title: March 2020: A Hedge That Didn't Hedge
body.scenario: In March 2020, as the COVID shock triggered the global "dash for cash" covered in Chapter 1, Bitcoin fell by roughly half in the space of about two days, a crash later nicknamed "Black Thursday" in crypto markets, falling right alongside global equities rather than offering shelter from the selloff.
body.prompt: An investor holding Bitcoin specifically as a hedge against an equity market crash would have been surprised by March 2020. Using what you know about the dash-for-cash dynamic from Chapter 1, explain why a supposedly independent asset fell in lockstep with equities during exactly the moment a hedge was needed most.
body.modelAnswer: The dash for cash in March 2020 was a scramble for the most liquid, immediately usable asset (US dollars), not a rotation into any and every alternative asset. Investors facing margin calls and redemptions sold whatever they could sell quickly to raise cash, and highly liquid, exchange-traded crypto was an easy, fast source of cash, so it was sold alongside equities rather than bought as a refuge. This is the same mechanism that hit emerging market assets, including Indian equities, in March 2020: a systemic liquidity shock does not discriminate between asset classes the way investors hope during calmer periods. An asset only behaves as a genuine hedge if its holder base and market structure are different enough from the assets being sold that it is not swept into the same forced-selling wave, and crypto in 2020 simply was not.

body.text: None of this means crypto can never decouple from risk assets in the future; correlations shift as an asset's investor base and market structure mature. It means that, based on the data through the period covered in this course, treating crypto as an uncorrelated diversifier during a systemic liquidity shock has been a costly assumption, not a reliably profitable one.

children.text: Indian investors trading crypto face one of the stricter tax treatments among major markets: a flat 30% tax on gains from virtual digital assets, with no ability to offset losses against other income or carry them forward, alongside a 1% TDS deducted on qualifying transactions. This framework was introduced from July 2022 under Section 115BBH (the flat 30% tax) and Section 194S (the 1% TDS) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. It adds a real, liquidity-independent cost and friction to trading crypto in India that does not exist for many global peers, which itself likely dampens some of the beta-chasing, high-leverage trading behavior that shows up more freely in other markets.

body.text: Section references above are to the Income-tax Act, 1961, as these provisions stood when introduced in 2022. The Income-tax Act, 2025 has since renumbered many provisions; confirm the corresponding current section numbers before citing them in any published material.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Based on this lesson, which statement best describes Bitcoin's typical behavior during a global liquidity tightening cycle?
options: It reliably rises as investors flee to it as a safe haven, just like gold
It tends to fall more sharply than broad equity indices, behaving like a high-beta risk asset rather than a hedge
It is completely uncorrelated with any other asset class
It is unaffected by global liquidity because it operates outside the traditional financial system
body.explanation: Despite the "digital gold" narrative, Bitcoin has historically fallen more sharply than broad equity indices during liquidity tightening, consistent with a high beta to risk assets rather than behaving as an uncorrelated or safe-haven hedge.

points: Despite the "digital gold" narrative, Bitcoin has historically behaved as a high-beta risk asset, amplifying rather than hedging global liquidity swings.
In 2022, Bitcoin fell roughly 64% versus roughly 33% for the Nasdaq and a roughly flat return for gold, illustrating very different sensitivities to the same tightening cycle.

High crypto beta comes from an investor base overlapping with speculative risk-on capital, high leverage through perpetual futures and on-chain borrowing, and a lack of a structural demand floor like central bank gold buying.

The March 2020 "Black Thursday" crash showed that a systemic dash-for-cash liquidity shock can hit crypto and equities together, undermining the idea of crypto as a reliable hedge exactly when a hedge is needed most.
India's flat 30% tax on virtual digital asset gains, with no loss offset, plus 1% TDS, adds a liquidity-independent friction to crypto trading in India that does not exist in many other markets.
